issues.description: The manuscript contains a severe contradiction regarding the sample. The abstract and introduction repeatedly claim the study uses a 'large, national probability sample' and a 'general population sample'. However, the Methods section explicitly states participants were recruited 'through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington' with an average age of 19. This completely invalidates the primary theoretical contribution of the paper, which was to test hypotheses in a general population rather than a student sample.
issues.quote: We expand on Stanley et al.’s study by using a large, national probability sample spanning five years to examine how these variables relate over time in the general population.

issues.description: There is a major conceptual mismatch between the measured items and the construct name used throughout the results and discussion. The manuscript refers to the dependent variable as 'willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment' and 'willingness to make sacrifices for the environment'. However, the actual items measured are 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'. These items measure environmental concern and belief, not behavioral willingness or sacrifice.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, “How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?” and “To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?”.

issues.description: The authors conclude that SDO is a stronger predictor of environmentalism than RWA. However, their own chi-square difference test comparing the constrained model (paths equal) to the unconstrained model was non-significant (p = .126). This means there is no statistical difference between the predictive strength of SDO and RWA. Concluding otherwise based on the 'pattern of unstandardized coefficients' is a fundamental statistical error.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.description: The authors state that reliabilities for SDO and RWA were 'poorer than is typically the case' but fail to report the actual reliability coefficients (e.g., Cronbach's alpha or McDonald's omega) anywhere in the text or in Table 1. This prevents readers from evaluating the psychometric quality of the measures.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31].

issues.description: The authors used listwise deletion for a 5-wave longitudinal study. This is highly inappropriate as it assumes data are Missing Completely At Random (MCAR), severely reduces statistical power, and introduces bias due to attrition. Modern missing data techniques like Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) should be used, especially since Mplus handles FIML by default.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: The authors note that one RWA item was not assessed at Time 2. Given they used listwise deletion, it is unclear how this structural missingness was handled. If the item was missing for all participants at Time 2, listwise deletion would result in a sample size of zero if the item was included in the model. The manuscript fails to explain how this was resolved.
issues.quote: The item “Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done”, was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: The authors constrained item residual variances to be equal over time, implying they used a latent variable cross-lagged panel model. However, they do not report testing for longitudinal measurement invariance (configural, metric, scalar). Establishing measurement invariance is a strict prerequisite before evaluating structural paths over time in latent models.
issues.quote: We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points.

issues.description: The authors report degrees of freedom (df = 2279) and item-level constraints that strongly imply a latent variable cross-lagged panel model. However, they never explicitly state whether the constructs were modeled as latent variables or observed mean scores. The exact model specification must be clearly described.
issues.quote: The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus... We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time

issues.description: The authors report a CFI of .86, which indicates poor model fit (typically > .90 or .95 is required). They dismiss this poor fit by claiming it is 'affected by model complexity' without providing sufficient justification or citing literature to support ignoring the CFI in favor of RMSEA and SRMR.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit...

issues.description: The authors report a chi-square difference of 15,389.13 for 1 degree of freedom when comparing the lagged effects between SDO and RWA. This value is mathematically absurd for a single constraint, especially given the small unstandardized coefficients (B = .02 and B = -.001) and the overall model chi-square. This indicates a severe calculation or typographical error.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)

issues.description: The authors state that full details about the sample are available on the NZAVS website. However, the NZAVS is a national postal/online probability sample of adults, whereas the described sample is an introductory psychology pool (N=374). This suggests a severe copy-paste error from another manuscript or a fundamental misattribution of the data source.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: For the RWA cross-lagged path, the authors report B = -.02, SD = .01, and a 95% CI of [-.05, -.01]. A 95% CI is typically calculated as B ± 1.96*SE. If the standard error (reported as SD) is .01, the CI should be approximately [-.04, 0.00]. The reported CI does not align with the estimate and standard error.

The text states a significance threshold of p < .05 was adopted, but the caption for Figure 1 states the threshold is p < .01. Furthermore, the justification that p < .05 was chosen 'Because of the large sample size' is illogical; larger samples typically warrant more stringent alpha levels (e.g., p < .01) to avoid overpowered trivial effects.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.description: The authors state they present standardized parameters, but the notation used in the results (e.g., 'B = -.11') typically denotes unstandardized parameters. Furthermore, if cross-lagged paths were constrained to equality over time, the unstandardized parameters would be equal, but standardized parameters would vary across time points. Reporting a single estimate implies it is unstandardized, contradicting their statement.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances.

issues.description: The authors highlight a bidirectional relationship where environmentalism predicts RWA over time. However, the unstandardized effect size is extremely small (B = -.01 on a 7-point scale). The practical significance of this finding is overstated in the discussion.
issues.quote: The lagged effect of willingness to sacrifice on both SDO and RWA were statistically significant and negative... B = -.01, SD = .002, p = .002

issues.description: The authors claim the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism is stronger than for RWA based on non-overlapping confidence intervals. While non-overlapping CIs imply a significant difference, comparing CIs is a conservative and informal method. A formal statistical test for dependent overlapping correlations (e.g., Steiger's Z) should be used.
issues.quote: Of note here is that the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval.

issues.description: The Data Analysis section contains a duplicated sentence regarding the constraint of cross-lagged associations.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. [...] Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.description: The authors use '2(1)' to denote the chi-square difference test, missing the delta and chi-square symbols (Δχ²).
